summary: The largest country in Africa by area, with most of its territory covered by the Sahara; it became independent in 1962 after 132 years of French colonial rule and a war of independence, and is rich in oil and natural gas.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: At the end of the 7th century Arab armies conquered North Africa; although resisted by figures such as the Berber queen Kahina, the Berbers gradually converted to Islam within a few generations, with the Maliki school becoming mainstream. French colonial rule (1830–1962) failed to change people’s faith, and in 1931 Ibn Badis founded the “Association of Algerian Muslim Ulema,” which combined Islam with national identity and became an important pillar of the independence movement. In the 1990s the government and Islamist armed groups fought a civil war that killed about 150,000 people, but Islam remains the shared faith and state religion of the whole country.

ranking.name: Islam (Ibadi)
ranking.description: Ibadism originated in the Kharijite movement of early Islam, and from 776 to 909 it established the Rustamid dynasty at Tiaret. After the dynasty was destroyed by the Fatimids, its followers moved south to the edge of the Sahara, and from the 11th century built five oasis towns in the M’zab Valley (around present-day Ghardaïa), forming a distinctive community consisting mainly of M’zabite Berbers; the valley is listed as a World Heritage site.

ranking.name: Christianity and others
ranking.description: Ancient North Africa was a Christian stronghold, as represented by Saint Augustine, born in 354 in what is now Souk Ahras, but after Islamization Christianity gradually disappeared. During the French colonial period about a million European settlers (pieds-noirs) were Catholic, and almost all left after independence in 1962. Today’s small number of Christians are mainly evangelical converts in the Kabylie region since the 1990s, and foreign residents.

religion.background: North Africa was a Christian stronghold in Roman times; after the Arab conquest of the 7th century Islam gradually replaced Christianity, the Berbers became Muslims over several centuries, and sects such as Ibadism appeared. From the 16th century the Ottoman Empire ruled Algiers, and after the French invasion of 1830 large numbers of Catholic settlers arrived, but the colonial government’s suppression of Islam instead strengthened Muslim national consciousness. After independence in 1962 Islam was made the state religion, and the civil war of the 1990s was a fierce conflict between Islamist politics and the secular military.

language.official: The official languages are Arabic and Berber (Tamazight).

ranking.name: Arabic (Algerian dialect)
ranking.description: The Arab conquest of the 7th century brought Arabic, and in the 11th century Bedouin tribes such as the Banu Hilal migrated westward in force, further Arabizing the countryside. The Algerian dialect (Darja) is Arabic-based, mixed with large amounts of Berber, French, Turkish and Spanish vocabulary. After independence in 1962 the government pursued a policy of “Arabization,” replacing French with Standard Arabic as the language of education and administration, but it is the dialect that is used in daily life.

ranking.name: Berber (Kabyle, Chaoui, etc.)
ranking.description: Berber (Tamazight) is the language of the indigenous people of North Africa, long predating the arrival of the Arabs, and is spoken mainly in the Kabylie region, the Aurès Mountains (Chaoui), the M’zab Valley and the Tuareg region of the south. The Arabization policy after independence suppressed Berber, provoking the “Berber Spring” of 1980 and the “Black Spring” protests of 2001, and Berber finally became a national language in 2002 and an official language in 2016.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French colonial rule from 1830 to 1962 made French the language of administration, education and the upper classes. Although the government pursued Arabization after independence, French is still widely used in higher education, business and the media, and many people use it fluently, but those with French as a mother tongue are only a tiny minority.

language.history: The earliest language of Algeria was Berber, and in antiquity there was the Tifinagh script. The Arab conquest of the 7th century and the arrival of Bedouin tribes in the 11th century made Arabic gradually the language of the majority, with Berber retreating to the mountains and desert. The Ottoman period left Turkish loanwords, and French colonization from 1830 made French the language of the elite. After independence, the Arabization policy and the Berber cultural movement long pulled against each other, and in the end the pattern emerged of Arabic and Berber as co-official languages with French still widely used.

ranking.name: Couscous
ranking.description: Coarse-ground wheat semolina is repeatedly steamed in a special steamer into loose small grains and topped with a broth stewed from lamb or chicken, chickpeas and vegetables such as pumpkin and turnip.
ranking.history: Couscous originated with the Berbers of North Africa; archaeological and documentary evidence shows it was widely eaten by at least the 11th–13th centuries, and Algerians call it “seksu.” It spread to Sicily and the Iberian Peninsula through exchanges in the Islamic world and, after French colonization, was brought to France and became a popular dish. In 2020 Algeria, together with Morocco, Tunisia and Mauritania, inscribed the knowledge and customs related to couscous on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list. It is indispensable at Friday family meals, weddings and funerals.

ranking.name: Chakhchoukha
ranking.description: Thin flatbread is baked and torn into pieces, then drenched in a rich sauce stewed from lamb, chickpeas, tomato and chili, and eaten after the bread has soaked up the broth.
ranking.history: Chakhchoukha originated with the Chaoui Berbers of the Aurès Mountains and the Biskra area in eastern Algeria, and its name is related to the act of tearing the bread. In the local pastoral and farming society wheat flatbread and lamb were the staples, and this dish is a way of turning everyday bread into a feast. It is made in large pots at weddings, Mawlid and family celebrations and is regarded as representative of eastern Algerian cuisine.

ranking.name: Rechta
ranking.description: Very fine handmade noodles are steamed and topped with a white clear sauce of chicken, turnip, chickpeas and cinnamon, mild and gentle in flavor.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Persian “reshteh” (thread); these fine noodles reached North Africa through exchanges in the medieval Islamic world and took shape in the urban cuisine of Algiers during Ottoman rule. Making noodles by hand is laborious, so rechta is a traditional dish that Algiers residents prepare only on occasions such as Mawlid, Ashura and the celebration of a baby’s birth, and it represents the urban food culture of the capital region.

ranking.name: Chorba
ranking.description: A thick soup cooked from lamb, tomato, onion and roasted green cracked wheat (frik), with coriander, mint and spices added.
ranking.history: The word “chorba” comes from Persian and entered North Africa through Ottoman Turkish. Green wheat, harvested before the grain is fully ripe and then roasted, is an ancient practice long known in the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa. This soup is the symbol of Ramadan in Algeria: at the sunset breaking of the fast each day, almost every household has a bowl of chorba as the first course, served with dates and bread.

ranking.name: Makroud
ranking.description: A shell made from semolina is filled with date paste and cut into diamonds, fried or baked, then soaked in honey syrup, crisp outside and soft inside, sweet but not cloying.
ranking.history: Makroud is popular throughout the Maghreb, and the version from Constantine in eastern Algeria is especially famous. Oases in southern Algeria such as Biskra abound in fine dates such as “Deglet Nour,” making dates an important ingredient of desserts. It is a treat that is sure to be prepared for Eid al-Fitr, weddings and family celebrations, traditionally made together by the women of the household and served to guests with mint tea.
